transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Logan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sanjay Rao (Polaris Insight), Elena Vazquez (Platform Eng), Tommy Li (CTO)

Summary:
Polaris Insight is evaluating Redwood for reserved/dedicated capacity with strict isolation and a burst model that requires some preemption/queueing controls. They want a predictable tail latency under burst, ability to hot-prewarm for scheduled campaigns, and firm controls for data residency/KMS. They asked about failure/fallback playbooks and cost tradeoffs vs. hosted and private deployments.

Topics:
- Reserved node topology, tenant fencing, and hot pools
- Preemption and preemptible instance semantics for burst capacity
- Queueing/backpressure and SLA implications
- VPC onboarding, KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML
- Benchmarking plan and POC scope

Action items (recorded here as notes):
- Quote, benchmark plan, sample model configs to be exchanged, schedule bench run.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Logan, our solutions engineer. Appreciate you taking the time, Sanjay, Elena, Tommy. Quick intros?
[00:15] Sanjay Rao: Yeah, hi, I'm Sanjay, we run infra at Polaris. We're trying to lock down plans for Q4 campaigns where inference spikes 8-10x for short windows. We need strong isolation and consistent p99s.
[00:28] Logan Ruiz: Great, that's exactly what we help with. Quick clarifying question — are you evaluating hosted first and then Dedicated, or do you want Private on-prem as well?
[00:39] Tommy Li: We're focused on Dedicated capacity but we want to understand when Private would be necessary. Cost, compliance, and latency are the big axes.
[00:50] Elena Vazquez: Also, our legal team flags full data residency sometimes. We'll need KMS and audit logs for certain workloads.
[00:58] Maya Chen: Good, we can show how Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with tenant fencing, and our Private option is for air-gapped or strict residency. Logan, can you walk through the preemption/burst options?
[01:10] Logan Ruiz: Sure. So with Dedicated you reserve nodes — think of them as hot GPUs that are only for you. We support a hot-pool prewarm for scheduled spikes, plus burst to a shared burst pool that can be preemptible. The preemptible nodes are lower-cost but can be reclaimed; we provide routing policies that fall back to either queued requests, lower-cost model variants, or hosted routes depending on your policy.
[01:34] Sanjay Rao: When you say queued requests, what's the typical delay? We can't have unpredictable tails during campaigns.
[01:42] Logan Ruiz: Under normal conditions queueing is millisecond-to-sub-second for short bursts if the hot-pool has some spare concurrency. For larger surges we have a configurable max-queue-time and SLA tiers. If you set a strict p99 SLA, we recommend sizing the hot-pool for the expected peak plus a 20% headroom and use prewarm windows.
[02:02] Elena Vazquez: Headroom is fine, but our finance team will push back on overprovisioning. What's the cost delta between reserving 20% headroom vs relying on preemptible burst?
[02:12] Logan Ruiz: Rough numbers: reserving headroom is roughly linear in monthly committed spend. Preemptible burst reduces committed spend by ~25-40% depending on usage pattern, but you accept some risk of preemption and routing fallback. We also have dynamic routing where less latency-sensitive routes go to cheaper quantized variants automatically.
[02:30] Tommy Li: Quantized variants — are those something you manage or we bring our own model?
[02:36] Logan Ruiz: Both. We can host a quantized variant we manage, or you can upload a quantized artifact. Our Optimize tooling will recommend quantization profiles by workload to minimize quality regressions.
[02:47] Sanjay Rao: For data encryption: we need customer-managed keys on KMS/HSM in our VPC. Is that supported in Dedicated?
[02:55] Maya Chen: Yes — Dedicated has KMS integrations. For Redwood Private we can also support HSM-backed keys in your environment. We'll attach our SOC2 docs; I can share the link after the call.
[03:05] Sanjay Rao: Please do. Also need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[03:09] Maya Chen: Noted — audit log forwarding is supported. We'll include the S3/ELK/Datadog examples.
[03:15] Elena Vazquez: Ok, technical question: how do you enforce tenant fencing? We're worried about noisy neighbors causing KV cache thrash or GPU memory contention.
[03:24] Logan Ruiz: We use a combination. Dedicated can be single-tenant nodes, or multi-tenant with strict cgroups + runtime fencing. For single-tenant you get physical isolation. For multi-tenant, we provide KV cache partitioning, per-tenant memory quotas, and scheduling priorities. We also support node pinning if you want full isolation for certain services.
[03:44] Sanjay Rao: Are there limits on model size for pinning? We run some 70B models occasionally.
[03:50] Logan Ruiz: We recommend dedicated nodes with appropriate GPU type for >70B. We can surface model memory requirements during onboarding and advise a node profile. Occasionally we shard KV across nodes but for very large models single-node GPU types or multi-GPU with NCCL/our runtime ops work best.
[04:05] Tommy Li: You mentioned routing fallbacks earlier — can you give a concrete example?
[04:10] Logan Ruiz: Sure. Example: you reserve n GPU slots for main traffic. During sudden spike, if hot-pool saturates and preemptible burst is unavailable, routing policy A enqueues requests up to X ms, policy B falls back to a quantized variant with lower cost and slightly lower accuracy, policy C routes a subset to Redwood hosted endpoints (if you allow cross-environment fallbacks). You can combine these with canary percentages.
[04:34] Sanjay Rao: Cross-environment fallback has compliance implications though. We can't send certain PII to hosted endpoints.
[04:40] Maya Chen: Right — fallbacks are policy-driven and you can mark routes as residency-sensitive so they never leave your Dedicated/Private footprint. We should capture which endpoints are residency-sensitive.
[04:50] Elena Vazquez: What's the onboarding time for Dedicated vs Private? Our ops timeline is tight — want production during peak in 8 weeks.
[04:58] Logan Ruiz: Dedicated can be provisioned in 2-4 weeks once contracts are signed and we have network details, images, and access. Private takes longer — usually 6-10 weeks depending on on-prem network approvals and HSM installation.
[05:12] Sanjay Rao: That feels tight. Can we start with a hybrid: small Dedicated pool + hosted for non-sensitive routes to reduce time to value?
[05:20] Maya Chen: Absolutely, that's a common path. We'll propose a hybrid POC in the scope doc.
[05:25] Tommy Li: For the POC benchmarks — we need Redwood to run with our model artifacts and our traffic shape. Is that doable?
[05:31] Logan Ruiz: Yes. We'll need model weights, sample payloads, and a traffic profile. Preferably not production data; synthetic or sampled data is fine. We'll run end-to-end bench with your top-K prompts and measure p50/p90/p99 and token cost.
[05:46] Sanjay Rao: On the subject of token cost — how transparent is cost per token for dedicated pools? We want predictability and to feed that into our billing system.
[05:54] Maya Chen: Our Console gives token-level cost breakdowns and per-route attribution. For Dedicated we can provide reserved capacity amortized cost plus per-token marginals for burst usage. We'll include sample reports.
[06:06] Elena Vazquez: Are there known failure modes for preemptible bursts? Like partial preemption causing requests to fail mid-stream?
[06:15] Logan Ruiz: We avoid mid-token failures; preemption is orchestrated around request boundaries. We drain any in-flight tokens where possible and route retries. The main issues are increased latency or fallback to lower-cost variants. We'll instrument tracing so you can see where fallbacks occur.
[06:31] Maya Chen: Quick note — sometimes the speech-to-text might show KV cash instead of KV cache in our internal notes, so take that with a grain.
[06:38] (brief chuckle)
[06:42] Sanjay Rao: A few operational questions: 1) How do autoscaling policies work with reserved capacity? 2) Can we set prewarm schedules tied to our campaign calendar? 3) Is there a hard cap to burst?
[06:53] Logan Ruiz: 1) Autoscaling on Dedicated is mostly scale-up within your reserved capacity and optional burst to shared capacity. We provide policy primitives: target utilization, cooldown windows, and priority tiers. 2) Yes, you can set prewarm windows in the Console — cron-like schedules or via API. 3) Burst is bounded by global pool availability; we give an estimated burst capacity during design and recommend purchase of transient burst credits for critical campaigns.
[07:20] Elena Vazquez: Burst credits? Explain.
[07:23] Maya Chen: Think of them as one-time prepaid capacity units you can redeem during high-impact events to guarantee capacity beyond what's available in shared pool. They show up in billing as usage lines.
[07:33] Sanjay Rao: Okay. Regarding SLAs — if we buy reserved nodes, do we get latency SLAs or just uptime?
[07:40] Logan Ruiz: We offer uptime SLAs and latency targets for Dedicated with proper sizing and monitoring. For strict latency p99 guarantees we do a sizing engagement and bake tail-latency targets into the contract.
[07:52] Tommy Li: Let's talk about failure/fallback playbook — what happens if a whole AZ loses private connectivity and our Dedicated nodes are affected?
[07:59] Logan Ruiz: We support multi-AZ deployments for Dedicated and automated failover. The typical playbook: route to capacity in another AZ/region (if allowed), spin up pre-warmed nodes in cold AZs if you purchased burst credits, or fall back to hosted endpoints for non-sensitive traffic. We'll also surface alerts in Console and provide playbooks for runbook automation.
[08:20] Sanjay Rao: Multi-AZ will be a requirement for production.
[08:23] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include multi-AZ diagrams in the follow-up.
[08:27] Elena Vazquez: About observability — what tracing hooks are available? We need per-request trace IDs and exports to our tracing backend.
[08:36] Logan Ruiz: Console supports distributed tracing headers and integrates with Jaeger/Zipkin/Datadog. We also export token-level cost and latency traces.
[08:46] Sanjay Rao: One more: are there guardrails to stop runaway costs for dev/test environments?
[08:53] Maya Chen: Yes, you can set per-route quotas, token caps, and alerts. Dev clusters can be on a cheaper compute profile with enforced caps.
[08:59] Elena Vazquez: On legal/compliance: what do you need from us for Private? Network diagrams, SOC2 contact, firewall allowlist?
[09:07] Maya Chen: Exactly. We'll send a VPC onboarding checklist: egress/ingress rules, peering, KMS endpoints, and the SOC2 package.
[09:15] Sanjay Rao: Great. If we're to sign for Dedicated, what are the typical contract terms? Minimum commit?
[09:22] Maya Chen: Terms vary. Common is a 12-month commitment with monthly billing for committed nodes, and optional burst credits. We'll attach a sample MSA and SOW.
[09:31] Tommy Li: For the POC — can we start with a 30-day reserved pool of small capacity and then scale?
[09:36] Logan Ruiz: Yes, we support short pilots. We'll outline a pilot configuration that mirrors your peak shapes scaled down.
[09:42] Sanjay Rao: Okay, a few more clarifications on the bench: 1) do you simulate sequence length distribution? 2) can you run KV cache warm/cold scenarios?
[09:50] Logan Ruiz: 1) Yes, we support custom sequence length distributions. 2) Absolutely; we can simulate cold starts vs warmed KV cache to show delta in p99 and token cost.
[09:58] Elena Vazquez: That will be important. Also, can the Console show per-model version rollouts and automatic fallback per version?
[10:05] Logan Ruiz: Yes — rollouts, canaries, and automatic fallback to previous model version if regression detected. We can also tie those to eval sets for regression alerts.
[10:15] Sanjay Rao: Sounds good. For the POC, we'll provide 2 model artifacts: a full-precision 30B model and a quantized 8-bit variant. We'll want you to test both under our traffic.
[10:25] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll coordinate. Logan, capture the benchmark checklist items.
[10:30] Logan Ruiz: Captured — model artifacts, traffic traces, sample prompts, expected p99 target, sequence length distribution, residency-sensitive route list, and campaign schedule for prewarm windows.
[10:41] Tommy Li: Any final risks we should call out now?
[10:44] Logan Ruiz: Main risks: under-sizing the hot-pool leading to tail spikes, reliance on shared burst without guaranteed burst credits, and cross-environment fallback incorrectly configured for sensitive routes. Mitigations: conservative hot-pool sizing for first campaign, run bench with warmed KV cache, and mark residency-sensitive routes.
[11:02] Maya Chen: Okay, recap and next steps: Maya to send quote + SOC2 + VPC checklist; Logan to send benchmark plan and request list; Sanjay to provide model artifacts and traffic profile. Schedule bench for next Tuesday (proposed).
[11:17] Sanjay Rao: We'll aim to get artifacts by tomorrow. Thanks everyone.
[11:22] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links.
[11:26] (call ends)
